subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation GNI stand for?
questions.explain: GNI (Gross National Income) is the total value of goods and services produced by a country plus income from abroad, often given per person.

questions.q: Which organisation devised the Human Development Index (HDI)?
questions.explain: The HDI was created by the UNDP to measure development using more than just wealth.

questions.q: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines life expectancy, education and which economic measure?
questions.explain: HDI is a composite index built from life expectancy, education (years of schooling) and GNI per capita.

questions.q: HDI values are expressed on a scale between which two numbers?
questions.explain: HDI is measured from 0 to 1, with values closer to 1 indicating a higher level of development.

questions.q: The infant mortality rate measures the number of deaths of children under one year old per how many live births?
questions.explain: Infant mortality rate is the number of deaths of children under one year old per 1000 live births in a year.

questions.q: Why is GNI per capita on its own a limited measure of a country's development?
options: It is an average that hides inequalities in wealth within a country
It cannot be calculated for developing countries
It only measures the health of a population
It is always the same as the literacy rate
questions.explain: As a mean value, GNI per capita hides the gap between rich and poor and says nothing about quality of life.

questions.q: Which of the following is a social indicator of development?
questions.explain: Literacy rate is a social indicator, whereas GNI, GDP and exports are economic indicators.

questions.q: A country records a high GNI per capita but also a low life expectancy and low adult literacy. What does this most likely suggest?
options: Wealth is unevenly distributed and not being spent on services for all
The country has no natural resources
The country must be highly developed in every respect
The GNI figure has been measured incorrectly
questions.explain: High income alongside poor social indicators points to inequality, with wealth not reaching healthcare and education for the whole population.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'development gap'?
options: The difference in wealth and quality of life between richer and poorer countries
The distance in kilometres between two countries
The gap between a country's exports and imports
The time taken to build new infrastructure
questions.explain: The development gap describes the widening difference in living standards between more and less developed countries.

questions.q: Which historical factor helped to widen the development gap for many poorer countries?
questions.explain: Colonial powers often exploited the resources and labour of colonies, holding back their long-term development.

questions.q: How can patterns of world trade keep some poorer countries poor?
options: They export cheap raw materials but import expensive manufactured goods
They export only high-value manufactured goods
They refuse to trade with any other countries
They import raw materials and export finished products
questions.explain: Selling low-value primary products while buying costly manufactured goods leaves poorer countries with an unfavourable balance of trade.

questions.q: Which physical factor can act as a barrier to a country's development?
options: A landlocked location with no coastline for sea trade
questions.explain: Being landlocked makes trade harder and more expensive, which can slow economic development.

questions.q: A country depends heavily on exporting a single primary commodity such as coffee. What is the main economic risk of this?
options: A fall in world prices would sharply reduce the country's income
The country would be unable to import any goods
It guarantees the country a stable, rising income
It removes the need for the country to develop industry
questions.explain: Reliance on one commodity leaves a country vulnerable to fluctuations in world market prices.

questions.q: Which of the following is a consequence of the development gap?
options: Migration of people from poorer to richer countries in search of work
An end to all international trade
A rise in the development of the poorest countries only
questions.explain: The gap in wealth and opportunity encourages migration from less developed to more developed regions.

questions.q: Bilateral aid is best described as aid given:
options: Directly from one country's government to another
Through international organisations such as the World Bank
In the form of loans that must be repaid with interest
questions.explain: Bilateral aid flows directly from one donor country to one recipient country.

questions.q: Multilateral aid is aid that is channelled through:
options: International organisations such as the World Bank
Private businesses in the donor country
questions.explain: Multilateral aid is given by donor countries to international organisations, which then distribute it.

questions.q: What is 'tied aid'?
options: Aid given with conditions attached, such as spending it on the donor's goods
Aid given with no conditions of any kind
Aid given only after a natural disaster
questions.explain: Tied aid comes with conditions, often requiring the recipient to buy goods or services from the donor country.

questions.q: Short-term (emergency) aid is best described as:
options: Food, water and shelter given immediately after a disaster
Long-term investment in schools and hospitals
Loans provided for building major dams
questions.explain: Emergency aid provides immediate relief such as food, clean water and shelter following a crisis or disaster.

questions.q: How does Fairtrade help producers in less developed countries?
options: It guarantees them a fair minimum price plus an extra premium
It removes all taxes on imported goods
It provides emergency food after disasters
It gives them free manufactured goods
questions.explain: Fairtrade guarantees producers a stable minimum price and a premium to invest in their community, reducing inequality.

questions.q: A charity supplies villagers with simple hand-operated water pumps that they can repair and maintain themselves. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Appropriate technology suits local skills, needs and resources so that communities can sustain it themselves.

specSource: CCEA GCSE Geography (2017) specification; Contrasts in World Development
